html:
An L-shaped hill over downtown Amman, the capital of Jordan, and among the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world. People lived here in the Neolithic, and the hill was fortified in the Bronze Age, about 1800 BCE. After 1200 BCE it became the seat of the kingdom of Ammon; the Amman Citadel Inscription, found here, is the oldest known text in the Ammonite language. The hill then passed under Assyria, Babylon, the Ptolemies, the Seleucids, Rome, Byzantium and the Umayyads. In Roman times the city, called Philadelphia, spread far below it, and the hill became its acropolis.

Most of what stands is Roman, Byzantine or Umayyad. The Great Temple, often called the Temple of Hercules, was built when Geminius Marcianus governed the province of Arabia (161 to 166 AD); a few of its columns stand again, and nearby lie three fingers and an elbow of a marble statue thought to have been about 13 m tall. A 6th-century Byzantine church reuses the temple's stone. On the upper part of the hill is the Umayyad palace built around 735 under the caliph Hisham for the local governor: a domed entrance hall with four arched recesses in the Sasanian manner (the dome is a modern rebuilding), a colonnaded street, a bath, a round cistern 16 m across, and a mosque.

After the Abbasids took power the palace decayed. The Ayyubids added a watchtower in 1220, but for most of the next centuries the old city was a field of ruins used by Bedouin and farmers. In 1878 the Ottomans settled Circassian refugees here, and modern Amman grew around the hill. The Jordan Archaeological Museum opened on the hill in 1951, and much of the site is still unexcavated.
